analysis.one_liner: Requires websites and apps used by employers, governments, and businesses to be accessible to people with disabilities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on March 3, 2026 with two Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has seen no further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that the Americans with Disabilities Act covers websites and apps — not just physical stores and offices. Employers, government agencies, businesses, testing companies, and the web developers who build for them would have to make their sites and applications usable by people who are blind, deaf, or have other disabilities. The Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission would write specific technical standards, update them every three years, enforce them, and set up a technical assistance center and grants of up to $10,000 to help small businesses comply.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans with disabilities. Under current law, courts disagree over whether the ADA even applies to the websites of businesses without a physical location, and the bill's own findings state that most web content of ADA-covered entities still contains significant barriers. The bill would set one clear, enforceable national standard, give people with disabilities the right to sue without first filing a complaint with an agency, and award attorney's fees and damages to people who win.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers, public entities, public accommodations, and testing entities to ensure their web content and applications are accessible, whether or not they have a physical location.

States that ADA coverage of public accommodations applies to all web content and applications regardless of any link to a physical place, resolving courts that have read the ADA as covering only physical locations.

Directs the Justice Department and the EEOC to issue proposed rules within 12 months and final technical standards within 24 months, and to update the standards every 3 years to keep pace with new technology.
Creates a private right of action in state or federal court without exhausting administrative remedies, with compensatory and punitive damages available and attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs.
Establishes a technical assistance center and grants of up to $10,000 for small entities to audit and fix inaccessible websites and apps, with delayed compliance deadlines for small businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Any employer, government agency, business, or testing company whose website or app is used in hiring, service delivery, or sales would bear the cost of auditing and remediating its digital content, along with the web development firms that build for them. Taxpayers would fund the authorized $35.15 million per year through fiscal 2036 for rulemaking, enforcement, the technical assistance center, and small-business grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Website operators, app developers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be a real cost for a very broad range of entities — the bill covers every employment use, government service, and consumer-facing business website and app — and private plaintiffs could seek compensatory and punitive damages, not just a fix.

The bill expressly forbids regulators from requiring a person to notify a business of a violation before suing, so an operator could face a lawsuit, with damages exposure, without any warning or chance to fix the problem first — the strongest good-faith objection to the bill's design.

The rulemaking timeline is aggressive — final standards due 24 months after enactment and applicable to large entities 30 days later — which could strain the Justice Department and leave businesses scrambling to meet standards written on a tight clock.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: people with disabilities are currently shut out of job applications, government services, and online shopping, and courts disagree on whether the ADA even reaches these sites. Clear national standards could also reduce today's wave of ambiguous ADA web lawsuits, since businesses would know exactly what to build to. The serious weakness is enforcement design — allowing suits without any pre-suit notice, with punitive damages — which raises the risk of demand-letter litigation aimed at extracting settlements rather than fixes. The bill's phased deadlines, small-entity carve-outs, grants, and 'undue burden' defenses soften but do not eliminate the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee in March 2026, and nothing has happened since — no hearings, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on March 3, 2026, joined by Sens. Markey and Warren as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
Two senators — both Democrats — have cosponsored the bill, and no further action has been taken in the committee since the March referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost: the bill is stalled at the committee stage. If it stays there, businesses and public entities remain free of new federal web accessibility standards, while people with disabilities remain without a clear federal remedy for inaccessible websites and apps.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed uniform web accessibility standards under the ADA.

for.name: 2 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors; no other senators have joined since.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred in March 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat, and no Republican has signed on; there have been no votes or floor action, so no partisan split on the merits has been recorded yet.

industries.industry: Websites, apps, and consumer-facing digital businesses
industries.note: These operators would bear the cost of auditing and rebuilding inaccessible sites and apps, plus damages exposure in private suits. That cost is the mirror image of the access people with disabilities would gain, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Web and software development vendors (the bill's 'commercial providers')
industries.note: They would face direct liability for building inaccessible products for covered entities, but the same mandate creates a large market for accessibility audits, remediation, and accessible design work.

They would still face the accessibility mandate, but with extra lead time (their compliance deadline is years after large entities), an 'undue burden' defense, and grants of up to $10,000 to fix their sites.

Firms offering exams, licensing, and certification courses online would have to make their platforms accessible or face suit; their cost is the access students and professionals with disabilities would gain.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, no committee activity since the March referral, and no apparent House companion movement, the bill is very unlikely to advance; most referred bills never receive a markup or floor vote. Its most realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress or being folded into a larger disability-rights package.
